content.title: Is April Fools’ Day the same as Día de los Inocentes? Here’s the truth
content.text: April 1, 2026Updated April 2, 2026, 8:29 a.m. MTThis April 1, don’t be surprised if you fall victim to a prank, as this date marks April Fools’ Day in the United States, the equivalent of Dia de los Inocentes in Latin America.April Fools’ Day is an event no one escapes. Pranks take center stage among family and friends, and thanks to today’s digital age, on social media as well. From telling a harmless lie to organizing an entire theatrical performance to make a “fool” out of your victim, the possibilities for pranking on this day are endless.For some Hispanics, April Fools’ Day may not sound familiar, but instead, they recognize Dia de los Santos Inocentes, which is observed every Dec. 28. Although both dates are the perfect excuse for laughs and small scares through pranks, their origins stem from different historical and religious events.What sets April Fools’ Day apart from Dia de los Inocentes? This is the story behind each of these dates.Origin of April Fools’ DayThere are several theories about the origin of April Fools’ Day that date back hundreds of years, according to almanac.com. One theory connects this day to an ancient Roman festival called "Hilaria," which took place at the end of March and during which people dressed up to imitate or mock one another.Another origin story says the date arose in 1582, when Pope Gregory XIII introduced the Gregorian calendar, leaving behind the Julian calendar that had been used since the era of Julius Caesar. Once the new system was adopted, King Charles IX of France changed the date of the New Year from April 1 to January 1, a sudden change that inevitably created confusion among some people. Those who forgot the new New Year date began to be called “April fools.” These people were pranked by being given mock gifts or invited to fake parties.What Is the Difference Between April Fools’ Day and Día de los Inocentes?In Latin America, it is common to observe Dia de los Inocentes by playing pranks, just like on April Fools’ Day. However, the date is December 28, and its origin story differs from the U.S. version.Día de los Inocentes originated from a Christian biblical event that recounts that when Jesus was born, King Herod I ordered the killing of all children under two years old in an attempt to end the life of the “Messiah,” fearing his power would be taken away. Because the king did not know who Jesus was, he ordered the deaths of all children who could be his age, triggering the massacre of hundreds of “santos inocentes” (holy innocents), according to the biblical passage.Additionally, the emphasis on pranks during Día de los Santos Inocentes was later influenced by the Feast of Fools, a celebration that took place between Christmas and New Year during the Middle Ages. This festival featured carnivals that included music, costumes, and mocking church rituals.
